We want to understand what you meant by "there was something near the bottom of one of the screens, some kind of action I think, though I couldn't quite tell what it was for", so let's go a bit deeper. Which of these best captures what you were pointing at?

A) The large black button labeled "Continue Shopping" which is visually prominent but seems counter-intuitive for a checkout page.
B) The greyed-out "Place Order" button which appears disabled or inactive at the bottom of the payment section.
C) The vertical stacking of the two buttons, where the "Continue Shopping" option is placed above the "Place Order" option.

turns.a: If I had to pick... probably B? I think. Though I'm not sure that's exactly it — it might be closer to another option, depending on how you're defining it. It's more of a general feeling than a specific thing. Other people might not even notice.

turns.q: When looking at that greyed-out "Place Order" button, what specific visual details make it appear disabled or inactive to you?
turns.a: I suppose... looking at the first screen, I wasn't quite sure where the action was. There was something that looked like it might be an action but I couldn't immediately read it as one. turns.q: What specific visual details make it difficult for you to recognize that element as a button rather than just part of the background?
turns.a: I suppose it was the coloring. Everything on the page was in roughly the same... palette, I want to say. Nothing really contrasted with anything else. So my eye didn't go anywhere in particular. I'm not sure if that's intentional — maybe they wanted a calm, quiet look — but it made it harder to find the action.

turns.q: When all those elements blend into that uniform color scheme, what specific visual markers do you normally rely on to separate the primary action from the rest of the layout?
turns.a: I think because buttons need to tell you they're buttons. When you look at a screen, you're scanning for the thing you're supposed to do, and usually the most prominent thing is that thing. If the button is the same shade as the background, it stops looking like a button and starts looking like a label or a decorative element. You stop registering it as actionable.

turns.q: What would that "Place Order" element need to look like visually for it to clearly stand out as an actionable button rather than just a label or decorative part of the layout?
turns.a: I think I'm saying the same thing in different ways. The coloring just makes everything look the same. I'm not sure what else to add.

turns.q: If you were fixing this, what specifically would you change about the coloring of the "Place Order" button?
turns.a: Something visible without effort. A filled button — a real background color, not a ghost or an outline. Text that's 16 pixels minimum. Sufficient contrast so it passes basic accessibility checks. It doesn't have to be dramatic. It just has to be legible and recognizable as an interactive element at a glance. That's the standard. This doesn't meet it.
